newsitem.title: DENMARK: FEATURE - Denmark's hippy experiment reaches quarter-century.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Denmark's hippy experiment reaches quarter-century.

text.p: Born as a squat 25 years ago and later dubbed a social experiment, the "free town" of Christiania is today a virtual institution and a tourist site drawing a million visitors every year.

The disused military citadel was occupied by a handful of hippies on September 26, 1971 and they were soon joined by hundreds more, pledged to build a new society of tolerance, democracy and environmental awareness.
"Within three or four months there were so many people it was too late for the government to do anything about it," said one of the original squatters, who uses the name "Asterix".
The anniversary is being marked by three days of music, theatre and exhibitions.

The Danish state, with a tradition of tolerance and a strong distaste for confrontation, never forcibly evicted the interlopers and over the years the Christiania community has won a large degree of public acceptance.

Organised within a system of house, area and general committees, the approximately 700 adults and 200 children govern themselves by consensus on everything from community finances to disputes between neighbours.
Christiania does not recognise Danish law and much public and official opposition to the commune stems from the open use and sale of marijuana there.
Stalls on both sides of "Pusher Street" display a range of the drug's many varieties, sold by weight or in ready-rolled cigarettes at between 10 and 40 crowns ($2-$8) apiece.
Some things are forbidden, however, even in Christiania.

There are bans on the use or sale of "hard" drugs, the carrying of weapons, violence, the trading of buildings or dwellings and the wearing of "colours", the identifying emblems stitched to the jackets of motorcycle gang members.
The community was invaded during the late 1970s by hard drugs dealers and prostitutes controlled by violent motorcycle gangs but in 1980 it fought back.
"The junkies were offered withdrawal treatment and the dealers thrown out," says the collective's guide booklet.
Today there is an uneasy truce between the visionaries of Christiania and the hash dealers, most of them from outside the commune and some still connected to the bike gangs.

Apart from the hard-drugs ban they are not allowed to operate near the children's play areas but Asterix says he and his fellows fight a constant battle to keep the dealers in line and he would rather they all left.
"There's lot of money being made and some heavy people involved, it's a big worry and we spend so much energy on this problem when we could be doing other things," he said.
Police leave the illegal traffic alone for most of the time but stage largely symbolic raids once in a while.

Many of the 3,000 visitors who throng Christiania on an average day come to buy drugs or use the cut-price bars, Asterix says, adding that the huge numbers of outsiders compared to the 900 residents detracts from the community atmosphere.
Despite problems, Christiania still functions after a quarter of a century and claims credit for some pioneering schemes.

The sorting of refuse into different recycling groups such as paper, glass, metal and organic waste for conversion to fertiliser was adopted in the collective long before the city of Copenhagen introduced the practice, said a veteran resident.
The principle of allowing marijuana sale or use within a specified area was also a concept being considered by cities elsewhere in Europe, she added.

Christiania itself, built some 300 years ago to strengthen Copenhagen's defences during a period of constant warring with nearby Sweden, covers some 35 hectares (86.5 acres) between a moat and a sea inlet, just east of the capital's centre.
Along its fringes wooden cottages nestle among trees and bushes and along waterside footpaths, giving the air of a village deep in the countryside.
At its heart are a former barracks and administration buildings which now house music venues, a children's theatre, restaurants, craft workshops, a radio station and a community newspaper.

There is a business restoring antique stoves and furniture and another building the distinctive Christiania Bike, actually a tricycle with a large carrier mounted over the two front wheels which can transport goods, children, or a wheelchair.
Among other enterprises, collectively run, are a vegetable market, blacksmith, printing press, carpenters, candlemaker and grocer. There is also a bakery, shoemaker, and a hairdresser.

Services include a health centre offering traditional and alternative medicine, a workshop teaching Yoga, Shamanism, Shiatzu and other spiritual techniques, social counselling, childcare facilities and an ecological advice centre.
Each resident pays a monthly fee of 880 crowns ($152) for electricity and water, communal services, maintenance and other collective outgoings.
Asterix seemed unsure if he would still be a Christianite in 25 years' time but thought that the community would still exist, a belief shared by Ulla, a professional guide to Christiania.
"We certainly intend to be here for another 25 years," she said.
And Christianites may still be negotiating with the government in an effort to decide the waterfront settlement's official status and future, as they have since 1971. ($1=5.788 Danish Crown)
